items.title: Calculating the Rate of Change of a Side Given the Rate of Change of the Volume

sections.normalized_html: A cube is shrinking uniformly at a rate of [MATH: 3\,\text{mm}^3/\text{s}.] How fast is each side of the cube shrinking when the volume of the cube is [MATH: 27\,\text{mm}^3?]
sections.readable_text:
A cube is shrinking uniformly at a rate of [MATH: 3\,\text{mm}^3/\text{s}.] How fast is each side of the cube shrinking when the volume of the cube is [MATH: 27\,\text{mm}^3?]

[IMG: /graphics/c1f32e592fb27e54135151de3eda8dbb]

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: x] be the side of the cube and [MATH: V] be its volume. We are given that [MATH: (dV)/(dt) = − 3mm^{3}/s.]

We would like to find [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm dt}] when [MATH: V=27\,\text{mm}^3.]

We start with the formula for the volume of the cube: [MATH: V=x^3]

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

[MATH: (d)/(dt)V|= (d)/(dt)(x^{3}); (dV)/(dt)|= 3x^{2}(dx)/(dt).]

Before we plug in the known values, we need to find the value of [MATH: x] when [MATH: V = 27\,\text{mm}^3.] We get

[MATH: V|= x^{3}; 27|= x^{3}; x|= 3.]

We can now plug [MATH: x=3] and [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d V}{\textrm dt}=-3] into the expression for [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm dt}.] This gives

[MATH: (dV)/(dt)|= 3x^{2}(dx)/(dt); − 3|= 3(3)^{2}(dx)/(dt); (dx)/(dt)|= − (1)/(9).]

Therefore, the sides of the cube are shrinking at a rate of [MATH: \dfrac{1}{9}\,\text{mm}/\text{s}] at the moment when [MATH: x=3\,\textrm{mm}.]

items.title: Calculating the Rate of Change of the Surface Area Given the Rate of Change of a Side (and Vice Versa)

sections.normalized_html: All of the edges of a cube are increasing at a rate of [MATH: 2\,\text{mm}/\text{s}.] How fast is the surface area of the cube changing when the volume of the cube is [MATH: 8\,\text{cm}^3?]
sections.readable_text:
All of the edges of a cube are increasing at a rate of [MATH: 2\,\text{mm}/\text{s}.] How fast is the surface area of the cube changing when the volume of the cube is [MATH: 8\,\text{cm}^3?]

[IMG: /graphics/a65c93604cef1ea0b21d874059b940b3]

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: x] be the side length of the cube, let [MATH: S] be its surface area, and let [MATH: V] be its volume. All of the variables change with time. In particular, we are given that [MATH: (dx)/(dt) = 2mm/s.]

We would like to find [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d S}{\textrm dt}] when [MATH: V= 8\,\text{cm}^3.]

We want to find the rate of change of [MATH: S] knowing the rate of change of [MATH: x.] So, we start with the formula for the surface area of the cube:

[MATH: S= 6x^2]

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

[MATH: (d)/(dt)S|= (d)/(dt)(6x^{2}); (dS)/(dt)|= 12x(dx)/(dt).]

Before we plug in the known values, we need to find the value of [MATH: x] when [MATH: V= 8\,\text{cm}^3.] We get

[MATH: V|= x^{3}; 8|= x^{3}; x|= 2.]

So [MATH: x=2\,\text{cm}=20\,\text{mm}.]

We can now plug the known values into the above expression. This gives [MATH: (dS)/(dt)|= 12x(dx)/(dt); (dS)/(dt)|= 12(20)(2); (dS)/(dt)|= 480.]

Therefore, the cube's surface area is changing at a rate of [MATH: 480 \,\text{mm}^2/\text{s}.]

sections.normalized_html: Water is being poured into a rectangular prism-shaped tank. The length and width of this tank are [MATH: 20 \textrm{ ft}] and [MATH: 15 \textrm{ ft},] respectively. If the height of the water increases at a rate of [MATH: \dfrac{1}{6}\,\textrm{ft/min}], determine the rate at which the volume of stored water increases.
sections.readable_text:
Water is being poured into a rectangular prism-shaped tank. The length and width of this tank are [MATH: 20 \textrm{ ft}] and [MATH: 15 \textrm{ ft},] respectively. If the height of the water increases at a rate of [MATH: \dfrac{1}{6}\,\textrm{ft/min}], determine the rate at which the volume of stored water increases.

[IMG: /graphics/796ce033c83a1fd48f83e0ad15fb4056]

sections.normalized_html:
We define the following variables:

  • let [MATH: L] and [MATH: W] be the length and width of the tank, respectively, and

  • let [MATH: h] and [MATH: V] be the height and volume of the water in the tank, respectively.

Note that [MATH: h] and [MATH: V] change with time, while [MATH: L] and [MATH: W] are constants.

We are given that [MATH: L=20\,\text{ft}, \qquad W=15\,\text{ft}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm dh}{\textrm dt} = \dfrac{1}{6}\,\text{ft}/\text{min}.]

We would like to find [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm dV}{\textrm dt}.]

The relation between the two time-dependent variables, [MATH: V] and [MATH: h,] is given by the formula for the volume of the water in the tank: [MATH: V = LWh]

We differentiate both sides with respect to [MATH: t,] treating both [MATH: L] and [MATH: W] as constants, and we get

[MATH: (d)/(dt)(V)|= (d)/(dt)(LWh); (dV)/(dt)|= LW(dh)/(dt).]

Finally, we can plug in the known values and get [MATH: (dV)/(dt)|= (20)(15)(dh)/(dt); (dV)/(dt)|= 300 ⋅ (1)/(6); (dV)/(dt)|= 50.]

Therefore, the water level is rising at a rate of [MATH: 50\,\text{ft}^3\textrm{/min}.]

Item 5 — Example: Calculating the Rate of Change of the Surface Area Given the Rate of Change of a Side (and Vice Versa)

Example Prompt:
All of the edges of a cube are increasing at a rate of [MATH: 2\,\text{mm}/\text{s}.] How fast is the surface area of the cube changing when the volume of the cube is [MATH: 8\,\text{cm}^3?]

[IMG: /graphics/a65c93604cef1ea0b21d874059b940b3]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let [MATH: x] be the side length of the cube, let [MATH: S] be its surface area, and let [MATH: V] be its volume. All of the variables change with time. In particular, we are given that
[MATH: (dx)/(dt) = 2mm/s.]

We would like to find [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d S}{\textrm dt}] when [MATH: V= 8\,\text{cm}^3.]

We want to find the rate of change of [MATH: S] knowing the rate of change of [MATH: x.] So, we start with the formula for the surface area of the cube:

[MATH: S= 6x^2]

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

[MATH: (d)/(dt)S|= (d)/(dt)(6x^{2}); (dS)/(dt)|= 12x(dx)/(dt).]

Before we plug in the known values, we need to find the value of [MATH: x] when [MATH: V= 8\,\text{cm}^3.] We get

[MATH: V|= x^{3}; 8|= x^{3}; x|= 2.]

So [MATH: x=2\,\text{cm}=20\,\text{mm}.]

We can now plug the known values into the above expression. This gives
[MATH: (dS)/(dt)|= 12x(dx)/(dt); (dS)/(dt)|= 12(20)(2); (dS)/(dt)|= 480.]

Therefore, the cube's surface area is changing at a rate of [MATH: 480 \,\text{mm}^2/\text{s}.]

Item 8 — Example: Calculating the Rate of Change of the Volume Given the Rate of Change of a Side

Example Prompt:
Water is being poured into a rectangular prism-shaped tank. The length and width of this tank are [MATH: 20 \textrm{ ft}] and [MATH: 15 \textrm{ ft},] respectively. If the height of the water increases at a rate of [MATH: \dfrac{1}{6}\,\textrm{ft/min}], determine the rate at which the volume of stored water increases.

[IMG: /graphics/796ce033c83a1fd48f83e0ad15fb4056]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We define the following variables:

- let [MATH: L] and [MATH: W] be the length and width of the tank, respectively, and
- let [MATH: h] and [MATH: V] be the height and volume of the water in the tank, respectively.

Note that [MATH: h] and [MATH: V] change with time, while [MATH: L] and [MATH: W] are constants.

We are given that
[MATH: L=20\,\text{ft}, \qquad W=15\,\text{ft}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm dh}{\textrm dt} = \dfrac{1}{6}\,\text{ft}/\text{min}.]

We would like to find [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm dV}{\textrm dt}.]

The relation between the two time-dependent variables, [MATH: V] and [MATH: h,] is given by the formula for the volume of the water in the tank:
[MATH: V = LWh]

We differentiate both sides with respect to [MATH: t,] treating both [MATH: L] and [MATH: W] as constants, and we get

[MATH: (d)/(dt)(V)|= (d)/(dt)(LWh); (dV)/(dt)|= LW(dh)/(dt).]

Finally, we can plug in the known values and get
[MATH: (dV)/(dt)|= (20)(15)(dh)/(dt); (dV)/(dt)|= 300 ⋅ (1)/(6); (dV)/(dt)|= 50.]

Therefore, the water level is rising at a rate of [MATH: 50\,\text{ft}^3\textrm{/min}.]
